comparator.name: Econometrics and Operations Research
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from VU Amsterdam's current official curriculum pages (English and Dutch), which list the 2026-2027 subjects of each year and link to the 2026-2027 study guide, corroborated by official VU course pages for the thesis, Econometrics III, Operations Research II and the first-year introductory course. The normalized target is the regular Econometrics and Operations Research bachelor; Econometrics and Data Science is a separate registry target (cp-000092) and is not reconstructed here. Years 1 and 2 are compulsory common cores of ten subjects each. The zero-credit SAM Programme EOR listed in year 1 carries no study load and is not a 180-EC component. Year 3 consists of a 30-EC minor (free profiling space, internship or exchange) preserved as open space, followed by a specialisation in Econometrics, Operations Research or Mathematical Economics and a 12-EC thesis in the chosen specialisation. The Econometrics specialisation is instantiated under the neutral route rule (see routeSelection). The official page lists Econometrics III, Mathematical Economics III and Operations Research III as the year-3 subjects; the specialisation course is Econometrics III and the other two are instantiated as the remaining 12 EC of year-3 course space, which is a valid pathway whether they function as compulsory subjects or as the restricted choices beside the specialisation course. Source limitation: the 2026-2027 study guide itself refuses automated retrieval, so individual EC weights could not be read from it directly. The 12-EC thesis is taken from the official thesis course page (2025-2026); every other course is recorded at VU's standard 6-EC course unit, which is confirmed for Mathematical Economics I and for Econometrics III in earlier official listings and is the only allocation under which ten subjects fill each 60-EC year and three courses plus the thesis fill the 30-EC second half of year 3. A human check of these weights against the 2026-2027 study guide is recommended.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Econometrics and Operations Research bachelor, whose current official curriculum lets students choose one of three third-year specialisations: Econometrics, Operations Research or Mathematical Economics. Econometrics and Operations Research are equally central to the programme's identity (both name the degree and both run through a compulsory I-II sequence), and neither is less specialised than the other, so no route is clearly more representative. Econometrics is selected by the neutral tie-break as the first specialisation in the order the official curriculum prints them. The choice was fixed before any UCR course selection and does not depend on UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Econometrics, optimisation & mathematical economics
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is organised around three strands that mirror the comparator's three fields: an econometrics and statistics sequence (Research Methods & Statistics, Probability & Statistics, Statistics & Experimental Methods, Machine Learning, Econometrics), an optimisation and algorithms sequence (Logic & Discrete Mathematics, Optimization Methods in AI, Decision-making in AI, Algorithms & Data Structures, Advanced Algorithms), and economic theory and finance (Introduction to Economics, Microeconomics & Behavior, Behavioral Economics, International Macroeconomics, Accounting & Corporate Finance), all resting on a mathematics spine. The label names the three strands rather than presenting the programme as a full econometrics degree, which it is not: UCR has one econometrics course and no dedicated mathematical-economics course, so 'mathematical economics' describes the formal economic-theory strand, not an equivalent of VU's three-course sequence.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to VU's Econometrics and Operations Research bachelor: a mathematics, probability and programming foundation carried into econometric estimation and forecasting, optimisation and decision-making under uncertainty, and formal economic theory with macroeconomics and finance as application fields, closing with the ethics of algorithmic decisions.
progression: Introduction to Programming and Mathematical Methods open the programme in semesters 1 and 2 and precede every course that formally or substantively depends on them. Logic & Discrete Mathematics in semester 1 supplies the discrete and logical foundations before Algorithms & Data Structures in semester 3, which in turn precedes Advanced Algorithms in semester 4. Linear Algebra and Probability & Statistics in semester 3 precede the numerical, optimisation and linear-systems work of semester 4, so linear and non-linear programming and state-space analysis are taught only after matrix methods. Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) and Probability & Statistics (semester 3) precede multivariate Statistics & Experimental Methods and Machine Learning in semester 5, which precede Econometrics in semester 6, so estimation theory builds on mathematical and multivariate statistics. Optimization Methods in AI and Advanced Algorithms run together in semester 4; the latter builds on Algorithms & Data Structures rather than on the optimisation course. Introduction to Economics in semester 1 precedes International Macroeconomics, Microeconomics & Behavior and Behavioral Economics, which build on it explicitly. AI Ethics is placed last, after the modelling and decision methods whose use it evaluates. Every course is offered in its assigned term and every formal prerequisite falls in an earlier semester.

alternatives.label: Econometrics, optimisation & sustainable energy systems
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum keeps the quantitative spine of mathematics, statistics, econometrics and optimisation, and replaces the finance, macroeconomics, behavioural-economics and algorithms courses of the closest match with a sequence on sustainability, climate, life-cycle analysis, renewable-system design, public economics and an applied sustainability research project. Neither strand dominates, so the label names both the methods and the energy-and-sustainability domain to which they are applied rather than presenting the programme as a sustainability degree or as the closest match relabelled.
alternatives.concept: An econometrics-and-optimisation programme organised around the evidenced application of quantitative methods to energy systems and sustainable production: forecasting and estimating energy-related quantities, optimising under uncertainty, and analysing renewable supply, life-cycle material and energy use, and the market failures that energy policy addresses.
progression: Introduction to Programming, Mathematical Methods and Sustainability Essentials I open the programme; Sustainability Essentials II follows in semester 2 as the formal gateway to Renewable System Design in semester 6. Linear Algebra and Probability & Statistics in semester 3 precede the numerical methods, optimisation and linear-systems courses of semester 4. Climate Change and Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy in semester 3 establish the substantive energy and production problems before Public Economics in semester 4 analyses externality-correcting policy and before the applied research and design courses of year 3. Research Methods & Statistics, Probability & Statistics, and Statistics & Experimental Methods with Machine Learning in semester 5 precede Econometrics in semester 6. Research in a Sustainable Delta in semester 5 is taken after the quantitative and sustainability foundations are complete, and Renewable System Design closes the programme after both. Introduction to Economics precedes Public Economics and Microeconomics & Behavior. Every course is offered in its assigned term and every formal prerequisite falls in an earlier semester.
alternatives.distinctness: The closest match treats macroeconomics, finance, behavioural economics and algorithm design as the application and methods context of econometrics and operations research. This alternative instead organises the same quantitative core around the programme's evidenced energy and sustainable-production questions. That choice removes eight courses of the closest match — Logic & Discrete Mathematics, Database Management Systems, Algorithms & Data Structures, Advanced Algorithms, Accounting & Corporate Finance, International Macroeconomics, Behavioral Economics and AI Ethics — and adds eight that the energy concept requires: Sustainability Essentials I and II, Climate Change, Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Renewable System Design, Research in a Sustainable Delta, Public Economics and Ethics. The two programmes therefore share sixteen of twenty-four courses and each contains 60 EC the other lacks, and the difference is a change of application domain and of the economics taught (public economics of externalities rather than macroeconomics and finance), not a reshuffle.

selection.assessment: The closest match owns the six generator-eligible interests that describe the programme's shared core: quantitative solutions to economic, business and financial problems, mathematical modelling for decisions, programming and quantitative analysis, the Econometrics specialisation selected as the comparator route, and the econometric analysis of economic and financial shocks, including their effect on interbank lending. The remaining six generator-eligible interests form four specific candidate directions, each assessed separately. Energy systems and sustainable production (renewable-energy variability and electricity prices; production optimised for lower material and energy use) is evidenced by the current curriculum page and by two direct programme interests, and UCR can implement it as a valid programme that shares only sixteen courses with the closest match; it is included as the second alternative. The Operations Research specialisation, with its hospital beds-and-staffing application, is rejected as not substantively distinct: every UCR optimisation, algorithms and decision-under-uncertainty course (Logic & Discrete Mathematics, Optimization Methods in AI, Decision-making in AI, Algorithms & Data Structures, Advanced Algorithms, Computational & Numerical Methods) is already in the closest match, so an OR-led programme could differ only by replacing economics with machine-learning courses that the OR evidence does not call for, or by adding a single public-health course; that would be a relabelled near-duplicate rather than a different route. The Mathematical Economics specialisation is rejected for the same reason: Introduction to Economics, Microeconomics & Behavior and Behavioral Economics are all of UCR's formal economic-theory courses and are already in the closest match, and UCR has no game-theory, general-equilibrium or dynamic-optimisation course that could make a mathematical-economics route different. Networks in economics is rejected as not feasible: UCR offers no network-economics or graph-theory course, and Networks & Operating Systems concerns computer networks, so a network-economics programme could not be built without substituting unrelated material. Production therefore stops at two alternatives.

blocks: Both are the programme's opening calculus course: differentiation, integration and differential equations used as the basis for all later modelling. VU's course goes further into analysis.
Both are the dedicated linear-algebra course: systems of equations, matrices, vector spaces and eigenvalues.
Both are the dedicated numerical-methods course: numerical root finding, differentiation, integration and the accuracy of algorithms.

Analysis II and Mathematical Reasoning continues rigorous analysis and proof. UCR's Advanced Calculus is not scheduled in either alternative and Logic & Discrete Mathematics treats logic and discrete structures rather than analysis, so the component is left unmatched.
Both are the mathematical-probability course: probability theory and discrete and continuous distributions. UCR's course also covers estimation and simulation.

Both are the first-year statistics course covering descriptive and inferential statistics and hypothesis testing. UCR's course is applied and paired with research design; VU's is a mathematical statistics course, so the correspondence is in subject and function rather than in mathematical depth.

Both are the introductory econometrics course built on linear regression, estimation and testing. UCR's single econometrics course also covers GLS and instrumental variables, which VU spreads over its later econometrics courses.

Academic Skills: Probability and Inference integrates first-year probability and statistics in an empirical application with conditional expectation, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. UCR has no counterpart integrating these specific foundations.

Econometrics II continues the econometric sequence beyond introductory regression. UCR offers only one econometrics course, which is already matched to Econometrics I, so this component is left unmatched.

Econometrics III covers panel data models, vector autoregressions, impulse responses and cointegration. UCR teaches no panel-data or multivariate time-series econometrics; Linear Systems treats impulse responses mathematically but not as econometric estimation, so no counterpart is claimed.
Both are the introductory programming course in which students learn to write and debug programs for quantitative problem solving.

Both are the first optimisation course of the programme, covering linear and non-linear programming. UCR's course frames optimisation within artificial-intelligence search and constraint satisfaction.

Operations Research II is an introduction to decision-making under uncertainty, from stochastic optimisation to Markov decision processes. Decision-making in AI likewise treats planning and optimal behaviour under uncertainty and resource constraints, though from an AI-planning rather than a stochastic-programming tradition.

Both are the programme's advanced algorithmic-optimisation course. Operations Research III concentrates on combinatorial optimisation, network flows and integer-programming solver methods; Advanced Algorithms covers advanced solution methods for optimisation problems more generally, so the match is in function and level rather than in every topic.

The introduction to Econometrics, Operations Research and Mathematical Economics surveys the three fields of the degree, including network optimisation and complexity. UCR has no course introducing these three fields together.
Both are the macroeconomics course: output, inflation, unemployment, business cycles and fiscal and monetary policy.
Both are the programme's first finance course. UCR's course combines corporate finance with the analysis of financial statements rather than concentrating on financial markets and investment.

Mathematical Economics I treats individual and market behaviour, decision-making under risk, welfare and game theory. Microeconomics & Behavior covers decision-making under uncertainty, strategic behaviour, general equilibrium and market efficiency, the same theoretical territory, though with less formal mathematical development.

Mathematical Economics II continues the formal economic-theory sequence. UCR's only advanced microeconomic-theory course is already matched to Mathematical Economics I, and Behavioral Economics and Public Economics are applied rather than mathematical-economics courses, so no counterpart is claimed.
Mathematical Economics III is an advanced specialisation course in formal economic theory. UCR has no counterpart at this level.

Both are the programme's ethics course addressing the responsible use of quantitative decision methods. AI Ethics concentrates on fairness, bias, accountability and privacy in algorithmic decision systems.
The Integrative Practical applies the programme's methods to business cases in small groups. No UCR course applies econometric and operations-research methods to integrated business cases.

The Advanced Practical continues case-based group work with reporting and presentation of quantitative solutions. Research in a Sustainable Delta is also a team project for an external partner, but it applies sustainability research rather than econometric and operations-research methods, so it is not claimed as a counterpart.
The minor is 30 EC of open profiling space with no fixed content. It is preserved as open space and not matched to any UCR course.
The bachelor thesis is an independent quantitative research project in the chosen specialisation. No scheduled UCR course is a thesis; UCR's optional independent research is shown in this row.

notes.text: The VU programme includes a more extensive sequence in econometrics (three courses up to panel data and multivariate time series), operations research (three courses up to combinatorial and integer optimisation), mathematical economics (three courses) and mathematical analysis, together with two integrative case practicals and a 12-EC quantitative thesis. At UCR, students can study mathematics, probability and statistics, one econometrics course, optimisation, algorithms and decision-making under uncertainty, and microeconomic, macroeconomic and public-economics theory, but UCR does not offer the same depth or sequence in econometrics, operations research or mathematical economics.
